extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate (or beginning graduate) students in real analysis / differential equations
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and worked examples of Picard's existence-and-uniqueness theorem for initial-value problems, followed by definitions, examples, and basic topology of metric spaces (metrics, balls, open/closed sets, boundedness). Useful for learning hypotheses needed for existence/uniqueness and basic metric-space reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picard's theorem hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The differential equation y' = F(t,y) admits a unique solution if F is continuous on a rectangle I×J containing (t0,y0) and is Lipschitz in the y (second) variable on that rectangle (with Lipschitz constant L). One can choose parameters (α, M, L, h, etc.) to produce an interval on which the solution exists and is unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof constructs an h>0 (often not optimal) depending on bounds of F and the Lipschitz constant so that Picard iteration is a contraction (L·α < 1 or analogous condition). The theorem gives existence and uniqueness on [x0 − h, x0 + h].

rubrics_metrics.name: Picard iterates as constructive approximations
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof provides explicit Picard iterates (f0, f1, f2, ...) defined by f_{n+1}(x)=y0+∫_{x0}^x F(t,f_n(t)) dt which converge uniformly to the unique solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Picard iterates not only prove existence but give a method to obtain the solution in practice (examples show recovery of the exponential via iterates); uniform convergence and continuity arguments justify passing the limit through the integral and differentiating to obtain the solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lipschitz condition (in y) ensures uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: Being Lipschitz in the second variable is a substantive hypothesis ensuring uniqueness of solutions to the initial value problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Lipschitz condition fails, solutions may exist but need not be unique (Example 6.3.5 gives an explicit non-unique case). In the proof uniqueness is shown by estimating |f(x)−g(x)| and using the Lipschitz constant to force the sup norm difference to zero (a contraction-type argument, e.g. requiring L·α < 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of F guarantees existence (Peano existence theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is continuous (but not necessarily Lipschitz) then at least one solution exists (Peano theorem), although uniqueness may fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts Picard (continuity + Lipschitz ⇒ existence & uniqueness) with Peano (continuity ⇒ existence only) and notes that if F is discontinuous one may have no solution (example using a discontinuous φ and Darboux's theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral-equation formulation / weak solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f is a solution to y'=F(t,y) with initial condition y(x0)=y0 iff it satisfies the integral equation f(x)=y0+∫_{x0}^x F(t,f(t)) dt; one may relax the derivative requirement and discuss weak solutions defined via the integral equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Heaviside/ramp example shows that the integral formulation can produce 'weak solutions' where the classical derivative may not exist everywhere; this viewpoint is useful when F has discontinuities or distributions are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric space definition (axioms)
rubrics_metrics.description: A metric d:X×X→ℝ on a set X must satisfy: (i) nonnegativity d(x,y)≥0, (ii) identity of indiscernibles d(x,y)=0 iff x=y, (iii) symmetry d(x,y)=d(y,x), (iv) triangle inequality d(x,z) ≤ d(x,y)+d(y,z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four properties are the precise desiderata for a distance function; the text gives geometric interpretations and emphasizes that intuition from Euclidean geometry can be misleading in general metric spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard metric on ℝ
rubrics_metrics.description: On ℝ define d(x,y)=|x−y|. This is the standard metric; properties (i)–(iv) are straightforward and the triangle inequality follows from the usual triangle inequality for real numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ℝ is mentioned as a metric space without qualification, this standard metric is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstandard metric via a monotone φ on ℝ
rubrics_metrics.description: One may define a metric on ℝ by d(x,y)=φ(|x−y|) where φ(t)=t/(1+t) (or any increasing function with suitable properties), giving a metric with all distances <1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Triangle inequality is more delicate but can hold if φ has appropriate properties (in exercises more general φ are considered). This shows metrics need not coincide with Euclidean intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclidean metric on ℝ^n (standard ℓ2 norm)
rubrics_metrics.description: For ℝ^n define d(x,y)=√(∑_{k=1}^n (x_k − y_k)^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The triangle inequality is proved using the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality applied to coordinate differences; this is the usual Euclidean metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma is proved by noting nonnegativity of sums of squares; it is used to establish the triangle inequality for the Euclidean metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrete metric
rubrics_metrics.description: For any set X define d(x,y)=1 if x≠y and d(x,x)=0. All distinct points are at distance 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discrete metric is a useful 'smell test' for general metric-space statements; when X is finite this is easy to visualize, but it has nonintuitive features on infinite sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremum (uniform) metric on C[a,b]
rubrics_metrics.description: On C([a,b],ℝ) define d(f,g)=sup_{x∈[a,b]} |f(x)−g(x)| (the uniform norm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a bona fide metric on the space of continuous functions on a closed bounded interval and is the metric used when treating C([a,b]) without qualification; it is central to the Picard theorem proof (uniform convergence and continuity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Great-circle (spherical) distance
rubrics_metrics.description: On the unit sphere S^2⊂ℝ^3 define the distance between x and y as d(x,y)=arccos(x·y) (or r·θ for radius r), where θ is the angle between rays from the origin through x and y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This metric gives the shortest travel distance along the sphere's surface and generalizes to spheres of arbitrary radius; triangle inequality proof requires trigonometry/linear algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subspace metric (restriction)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (X,d) is a metric space and Y⊂X then the restriction d|_{Y×Y} is a metric on Y (the subspace metric).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating Y as a metric space one usually simply write d for the metric on Y; many properties (open/closed sets) depend on which ambient space is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundedness and diameter equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset S⊂X is bounded iff there exists p∈X and B>0 with d(p,x) ≤ B for all x∈S; equivalently diam(S)=sup_{x,y∈S} d(x,y) < ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ℝ with the standard metric is unbounded, while ℝ with the discrete metric is bounded. Alternative equivalent formulations are given and left as exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open and closed set definitions / balls
rubrics_metrics.description: Open ball B(x,δ)={y∈X : d(x,y)<δ}; closed ball C(x,δ)={y : d(x,y) ≤ δ}. A set V⊂X is open if for every x∈V there exists δ>0 with B(x,δ)⊂V. A set E⊂X is closed if its complement is open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open sets intuitively do not include their boundary. The text proves that open balls are open and closed balls are closed (exercise). Which metric space one is in matters for whether a particular set is open/closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of open sets in subspaces
rubrics_metrics.description: U⊂Y is open in the subspace Y (with the subspace topology) iff there exists an open set V⊂X such that U = V ∩ Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why a set can be open in a subspace but not open in the larger ambient space; the chapter gives examples and an exercise to finish the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union and intersection rules for open/closed sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Arbitrary unions of open sets are open; finite intersections of open sets are open. Dually, arbitrary intersections of closed sets are closed; finite unions of closed sets are closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These basic topological closure properties are proved/proposed as exercises and illustrated with counterexamples showing arbitrary intersections of open sets need not be open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hausdorff metric on bounded subsets
rubrics_metrics.description: For nonempty bounded subsets A,B⊂X define d_H(A,B)=max{ sup_{a∈A} d(a,B), sup_{b∈B} d(b,A) } (where d(a,B)=inf_{b∈B} d(a,b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the set of bounded nonempty subsets this yields a pseudometric (d_H satisfies (i),(iii),(iv) and d_H(A,A)=0); exercises ask to show it can fail to be a metric (distinct sets with d_H=0) and related properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing new metrics via monotone subadditive φ
rubrics_metrics.description: If (X,d) is a metric space and φ:[0,∞)→[0,∞) is increasing, φ(0)=0 iff t=0, and subadditive (φ(s+t) ≤ φ(s)+φ(t)), then d'(x,y)=φ(d(x,y)) is a metric on X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives the φ(t)=t/(1+t) example and an exercise to verify the metric properties for more general φ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-space metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: If (X,d_X) and (Y,d_Y) are metric spaces, then metrics on X×Y such as d((x1,y1),(x2,y2))=max{d_X(x1,x2), d_Y(y1,y2)} (or sums) define a metric on the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises ask to verify metric properties for these constructions; product metrics allow combining spaces while preserving metric axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function-space metrics via integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: One can define metrics on spaces of continuous functions by integrals, e.g. d(f,g)=∫_{0}^{1} φ(|f(x)−g(x)|) dx with φ positive continuous, yielding a metric on X=C([0,1]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises ask to show continuity and metric properties; such metrics differ from the uniform metric but are useful in many contexts (e.g., L^p-type constructions).
